appraisal_events.evidence: « elle se détourna, et d’un air indifférent et dédaigneux, se plaça de côté » ; ses regards « avec une fixité et un sourire dissimulé, que je ne pouvais interpréter d’après les notions que l’on m’avait données sur la bonne éducation que comme une preuve d’outrageant mépris » ; le geste dont « le petit dictionnaire de civilité que je portais en moi ne donnait qu’un seul sens, celui d’une intention insolente ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Gilberte's averted, disdainful look and her gesture are received by the boy as open contempt, leaving him humiliated and shut out of "l’inconnu de sa vie où je n’entrerais pas". The mature narrator ironizes the reading itself by attributing it to a child's "petit dictionnaire de civilité", so the contempt is staged as the boy's certainty rather than as an endorsed fact, while its humiliating effect is fully narrated.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ma tante devait parfaitement savoir qu’elle ne reverrait pas Swann, qu’elle ne quitterait plus jamais la maison » ; « ce grand renoncement de la vieillesse qui se prépare à la mort, s’enveloppe dans sa chrysalide » ; sa réclusion donne « à l’inaction, à l’isolement, au silence, la douceur réparatrice et bénie du repos ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The closing paragraph narrates Léonie's passage into definitive withdrawal: her sincere promise to revisit Tansonville is emptied by failing strength, and she is placed among lives that have stopped seeking one another. The narrator endorses the diminishment but inflects it as blessed rest rather than suffering, which keeps the polarity mixed.

status_effects.explanation: He is left with a "cœur humilié" that can only fantasize about insulting her, and his desire is reorganized as a wish to level himself with her or drag her down.
The scene fixes him outside her sphere: the "familiarité" of those who live with her is painful to him, and her world is "un bonheur inaccessible aux enfants de mon espèce".
She holds the local leverage: she looks, smiles, and walks off unanswered, while he is petrified and supplicating; only her mother's despotic tone briefly checks her ascendancy.

Her name works as a talisman that gilds everything attached to her — her grandparents, the "sublime profession d’agent de change", the Champs-Élysées quarter — raising her sphere into something enchanted and unreachable.
She passes into permanent reclusion, knowing she will not see Swann or leave the house again, though the narrator presents the isolation as restorative rather than punitive.

ambiguities: The child's reading of Gilberte's fixed look and gesture as "outrageant mépris" and "intention insolente" is explicitly attributed to the "petit dictionnaire de civilité" he carries in himself, leaving open that the gesture solicited rather than rejected him; E1 is therefore annotated as an experienced snub with ironized narrative stance rather than as narrator-endorsed contempt.

The "dame en blanc" who commands Gilberte is unnamed in the passage and is resolved to Odette only inferentially, through the grandfather's aside about Swann being sent away so that "elle" can stay alone with Charlus.
